Zelensky confirmed that Ukrainian forces managed to shoot down only one ballistic missile during the attack , citing a deficit of interceptor missiles for Patriot systems. The strikes triggered repeated explosions across Kyiv. Law enforcement officials reported that the strikes and resulting debris caused damage across seven of the city’s districts , affecting 18 apartment and private residential buildings, a medical clinic, a film studio, supermarkets, and educational institutions, and killing nine people. The AfD is designated as a “suspected” extremist group by German intelligence. Photo / AFP With elections scheduled across Europe next year, the striking success of the party, Alternative for Germany, could be a harbinger of further far-right victories, according to analysts, as well as a template for how they can be engineered. When a far-right party won a landslide victory on Sunday (Monday NZT) in a small state in eastern Germany, its reverberations could be felt from Downing Street in London to the Élysée Palace in Paris. Rarely has the result of a regional election been viewed with such portent for the fate of democracy in Europe. This wasn’t just any European country; it was Germany, a country that has relentlessly isolated far-right political parties since the calamity of Nazism. And it wasn’t just a strange outlier, but rather the latest step in a steady, decade-long march that has brought the far right ever closer to the fulcrum of power in Europe. With elections scheduled across Europe next year, the striking success of the party, Alternative for Germany, could be a harbinger of further far-right victories, according to analysts, as well as a template for how they can be engineered. Its populist, anti-immigrant message echoes those of nationalist leaders in Britain, France, Italy and Spain, all countries where voters harbour many of the same grievances as those in Germany. French voters will elect a new president next spring. An election is due in Spain by August, and in Italy by the end of next year. Far-right candidates are surging in all of them, threatening incumbents blamed for systemic problems with their countries’ economies. Advertisement Advertise with NZME. “Developed Europe is going through a version of sophisticated state failure,” said Mujtaba Rahman, an analyst who specialises in Europe at Eurasia Group, a political risk consultancy. “Governments are unable to address cost-of-living concerns. They are not able to deliver for their voters.” In Germany, rising prices and high unemployment helped win the far-right party, known by its German initials, AfD, more than twice the number of votes as Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s centre-right incumbent party. Because the AfD appeared to fall just short of an outright majority, according to near-final results, it may not end up governing Saxony-Anhalt, the state where the election was held. Rival parties have vowed that they would not form a coalition government with the AfD, whose leaders have used Nazi slogans and minimised the Holocaust. The AfD is designated as a “suspected” extremist group by German intelligence, partly because the group portrays Germans of immigrant backgrounds as second-class citizens. Advertisement Advertise with NZME. Still, the result could hobble Merz if members of his party blame him for the loss, at a time when Germany’s leadership in Europe was already faltering. Merz’s standing has deteriorated so badly that political analysts talk openly of his ouster, a once-far-fetched scenario in German politics. “It’s a big concern in Europe,” said Rahman, who previously worked for the European Union’s civil service. “A weak Germany, with a chancellor who is coming unstuck and being forced to deal with domestic problems, is bad and will ultimately subtract from Europe’s ability to confront its challenges.” Worries among centrists about France, where President Emmanuel Macron will step down next spring, are no less acute. Marine Le Pen, the candidate of France’s main far-right party, the National Rally, holds a commanding lead in first-round polls, and has even finished first in recent second-round matchups. That puts her closer to power than at any time in her 14 years of seeking the presidency. Marine Le Pen, the candidate of France’s main far-right party, is closer to power than at any time in her 14 years of seeking the presidency. Photo / Dmitry Kostyukov, The New York Times A far-right government in Paris, Rahman said, would destabilise the European Union in a way that no other national election has, given France’s size, nuclear arsenal and founding role in the European project. It might also bring an end to the so-called cordon sanitaire, under which mainstream parties in France, as in Germany, have refused to enter governing coalitions with the far right. “In both countries, the antifascist front that had prevailed since the end of the Second World War seems on the verge of collapse,” said Philippe Marlière, a professor of French and European politics at University College London. In Spain, analysts said the far-right Vox Party could elbow its way into the next coalition government, with the current Socialist-led government tarnished by corruption scandals and an immigration crisis. In Britain, the governing Labour Party ousted its unpopular prime minister, Keir Starmer, in July to try to regain traction against a fast-rising far-right party, Reform UK. Still, the rise of the far right is not inexorable. Reform’s success has been rudely interrupted by a series of financial scandals involving its firebrand leader, Nigel Farage. That has given the Labour government, under a new prime minister, Andy Burnham, some breathing room. In April, the far-right leader of Hungary, Prime Minister Viktor Orban, was swept out of power after 16 years , a casualty of widespread perceptions that his government was corrupt, inattentive to the economy, and had picked needless battles with the European Union. The defeat of his Fidesz party gave hope to mainstream politicians that the far right, too, is vulnerable. Advertisement Advertise with NZME. The extent to which those mainstream politicians “need to worry” about the AfD’s success, said Timothy Bale, a professor of politics at Queen Mary University of London, “is going to depend on whether, if it ends up in office, it behaves relatively normally, and whether or not it’s able to run things competently”. Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, whose populist party has neofascist roots, offers a playbook to other like-minded leaders. Having modulated her tone on issues like Ukraine and the European Union, she recently celebrated her government becoming the longest continuously serving in the history of the Italian Republic. Meloni is in a decent position to extend that run when she faces voters next summer. But the rising profile of a rival even further to her right, Roberto Vannacci, has led her to harden her positions on issues like immigration. Meloni heaped criticism on Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, after a sudden influx of migrants from Morocco into a Spanish territory in late July. Santiago Abascal (centre), leader of Spain’s far-right Vox political party. Photo / Finbarr O’Reilly, The New York Times Farage risks being similarly outflanked in Britain. Rupert Lowe, a disaffected member of his party, defected to start an even more right-wing group that is siphoning votes from Farage. Given that competition, and the proliferating questions about Reform’s finances, Bale said it was difficult to see how Farage could cobble together enough votes to form a government. In France, Le Pen’s path to power is more plausible. Her poll numbers are more than double those of the leading centrist, Edouard Philippe, or the leading far-left candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon. The big question in France is whether Philippe or anyone else will be able to gather enough support from the centre right and left to emerge as the consensus mainstream candidate. In a second round of voting, analysts said, such a candidate would stand a chance of beating Le Pen. But if France’s centre remains fractured, as it is now, that would give Mélenchon a shot at making the second round, likely facing off against Le Pen. In that scenario – one that France’s political establishment views as a nightmare – Le Pen would be the odds-on victor. Like other far-right leaders in Europe, Le Pen has kept her distance from US President Donald Trump. But she and other populist candidates could be buffeted by him anyway, according to analysts. Trump remains deeply unpopular in Europe and is fast losing popularity in the United States as well. The lesson that Europe’s beleaguered centrists hope voters will take from America’s turmoil, Rahman said, is that “if you experiment with non-mainstream parties, you risk making mistakes”. https://www.politico.eu/article/cyprus-a.text: The president of Cyprus wrote to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen calling for the EU to resume talks on its mutual defense clause. “I cannot overstate the importance of this provision for the EU and its Member States, especially in times of geopolitical uncertainty,” Nikos Christodoulides wrote in a letter dated Oct. 20 addressed to von der Leyen, seen by POLITICO. Article 42.7 of the Lisbon Treaty states that if an EU member is faced with "armed aggression," other members have an obligation to provide "aid and assistance by all the means in their power." Advertisement Advertisement The defense clause article had risen up the agenda because of mounting geopolitical threats, including U.S. President Donald Trump’s undermining of the transatlantic alliance, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and hybrid warfare campaign against the EU, and wars in the Middle East. “Given the gravity of the challenges we face, Cyprus would welcome the resumption of discussions at the relevant preparatory bodies. I would therefore appreciate an update on the proposals under consideration, as well as a timeline for the next steps,” Christodoulides wrote. The EU gamed out how the clause would work in practice with exercises earlier this year. Cyprus’ six-month presidency of the European Council, which ended on June 30, prioritized the issue after Iranian drones struck a British base on Cypriot soil in March. But the topic has largely fallen off the bloc’s radar, as the EU turns its attention to negotiating its seven-year, almost €2 trillion budget and finding more funding for Ukraine. Article 42.7 is not scheduled to be discussed at any European leaders’ summits in the foreseeable future, confirmed an EU official, granted anonymity to speak freely.
